title: The 9-Word Email (reactivation of dormant leads)
market: Any business with dormant inquiries; examples given for real estate, yacht brokerage, apparel, plumbing, B2B
funnel_position: win-back / lead reactivation (sequence role: win-back)
excerpt: Subject: Jason | Body: Are you still looking for a house in Georgetown? (Template: 'Are you still looking for [the thing they inquired about]?'; variation: 'Would you like to get started on your book this month?')

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a reply (not a purchase) to a lapsed inquirer on the promise that the sender still remembers their original request, because a one-line personal question is answered where a brochure is ignored.
structure.hook: First-name-only subject line; the body is a single question that restates the prospect's own original request.
structure.mechanism: Removes every marketing signal (no HTML, no pitch, no links) so the email reads as a personal note and the only possible action is to reply.
structure.big_idea: Re-engagement is a question, not a campaign.
structure.close: The question itself is the close; no sign-off pitch.
structure.voice_notes: Nine words, second person, conversational; the author warns it fails as cold outreach and must lead with help, not a pitch.

results.detail: Author-stated anecdotes, quoted as written: real estate client 'got dozens of replies and tons of engagement' and 'sold several other properties over the next couple of months'; motorcycle-jeans maker 'sold over $9,000 in less than a week'; yacht broker 'uncovered a buyer for a $100 million custom yacht'; postcard company 'went from 5% click-through to over 30%'; author says 'it's not uncommon to send emails that get 60%+ response rates'. No sample sizes or independent verification.

losing_variants.description: Author's description of the client's prior HTML marketing emails to the same list
losing_variants.result: '3% to 5% click-through rate' per the author, versus 'over 30%' for the nine-word email (self-reported).

lessons: Win-back email 1 of 3 in the standard (nine words, no links) has a documented originator and wording pattern: restate the prospect's original request as a yes/no question.
Reply is a valid CTA; a win-back that asks for nothing but an answer outperforms one that asks for a click (self-reported).
The device fails on cold lists; it depends on a prior inquiry the reader remembers.
notes: Primary source is the author's own blog; figures are vendor anecdotes. Variation 'Would you like to get started?' is for offers with a time element.

title: Copyhackers weekly newsletter: seven subject-line split tests (Jan-Feb 2013)
market: Startup founders and marketers learning conversion copywriting
funnel_position: daily/weekly content email to owned list (sequence role: daily)
excerpt: Winning subject: 'heart your home page [Copyhackers]' | Losing subject: 'how to show your home page some love [Copyhackers]'

structure.argument_sentence: This sells an open to a subscriber on the promise of a specific, quirky payoff, because a compressed, odd phrasing with the brand tag beat the plain how-to phrasing of the same content.
structure.hook: Short, slightly odd verb phrase ('heart your home page') with brand name in brackets.
structure.mechanism: Subject line is the only variable; body identical.
structure.voice_notes: Lowercase, playful, question-led subject lines; brand tag appended.

results.detail: Seven tests reported as winner's margin over loser in open rate: 7%, 4.6%, 4.4%, 4.2%, 2%, 1.5%, 0.9%. Follow-up brand-tag test: 'startup Qs about landing pages + emails [Copyhackers]' 36.4% open vs the same line without the tag 32% open. No sample sizes stated; the author treats these as directional.

losing_variants.result: lost by 7% open rate to 'heart your home page [Copyhackers]'

losing_variants.description: 'which home page kills it? a comparative analysis [Copyhackers]'
losing_variants.result: lost by 4.6% to 'possibly the most overlooked home page opportunity in the universe...?'
lost by 4.4% to 'when it comes to email, does size matter? [CopyHackers.com]'

losing_variants.description: 'increasing paid conversions by 61% on a product catalog'
losing_variants.result: lost by 4.2% to 'increasing paid conversions by 61% on a typical startup site'

losing_variants.description: 'does the tone of your copy really matter? [CopyHackers.com]'
losing_variants.result: lost by 2% to 'how the right tone turned around this small biz [CopyHackers.com]'

losing_variants.description: 'startup Qs about landing pages + emails' (no brand tag)

lessons: Subject lines that name the reader's situation ('typical startup site') beat the same promise aimed at a segment the reader is not in ('product catalog').
A question that leaves the answer open ('does size matter?') beat the line that gives the answer away ('no, size doesn't matter').
Appending the sender's brand to the subject raised opens on a warm list; a usable test for the subject-written-last step.
notes: Results are margins, not absolute rates, except the brand-tag follow-up. Newsletter body not evaluated.

title: Parallel Welcome Sequence (welcome email 'The Dark Room' and linker pages)
market: Copywriters and marketers who want to learn email copy
funnel_position: welcome sequence after opt-in (sequence role: welcome)
excerpt: Headline claim: the sequence 'Gets Up To 200% Engagement From Your New Subscribers'. Homepage: 'My welcome email is just the start of a ridiculous email adventure involving time-travel, giant lions, robot AI invasions...'

structure.argument_sentence: This sells continued reading (and later products) to a new copywriting subscriber on the promise of an entertaining serial, because every email's only CTA is a 'time-travel remote' link that delivers the next email instantly and routes the keenest readers to parallel web pages that carry bonuses and offers.
structure.hook: A welcome email written as a disturbing/funny scene ('The Dark Room') rather than a deliverable and intro.
structure.mechanism: Three rules: every email carries a link that fires the next email immediately (otherwise 24h interval); that link is the sole CTA woven into the story; each link lands on a 'linker webpage' forming a parallel series seen only by engaged readers, used for bonus content and sales.
structure.big_idea: A welcome sequence the reader can binge, so the most engaged readers consume twice the content of a linear series.
structure.close: Each email ends on the remote link; the author recommends at least ten emails.
structure.voice_notes: First person, self-mocking Australian persona ('Australia's best copywriter'), serialized fiction mixed with copy tips; long emails read in one sitting.

results.detail: Author states 'up to 200% readership' defined as relative content consumed versus an email-only series, 'not 200% OPEN RATES'; one subscriber's session described as 'NINETY-TWO MINUTES'; open-rate comparison shown only as an unlabelled graph image; deliverability claim from 'my own (unscientific) tests'. No revenue stated. Testimonials attributed to initials only.

lessons: A welcome sequence can make 'open the next one' the CTA of every email; the standard's rule that every non-final email ends with a reason to open the next has a working extreme here.
Segment by behaviour inside the copy: the readers who click the loop get the offers, the rest get the plain sequence.
Story-led welcome email for a sophistication-4 market (copywriters who have seen every 'here's your freebie' email).
notes: Email text is gated behind opt-in; annotation is from the author's public description page and homepage. Named in docs/03 Section 12.

title: The Power Trio: Big Reveal, Free Taste, Last Chance launch emails
author_or_company: Ramit Sethi / I Will Teach You To Be Rich
market: Personal finance, career and online-business course buyers
funnel_position: launch: open cart, mid-cart sample, cart close (sequence roles: open cart, mid-cart, cart close)
excerpt: Headline: '3 sales emails worth $379,643'. The Big Reveal introduces the product; the Free Taste (a Judge Judy story plus a free sample lesson) gets readers to try it; the Last Chance is 'a brief courtesy reminder so readers don't miss out'.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a course to a warmed list on the promise that they can see the product work before buying, because the three emails move from the idea (reveal) to a demonstration (free sample) to a deadline (last chance) without pressure language.
structure.hook: Big Reveal opens with a discussion of what separates successful people, not with the product.
structure.mechanism: Sequence of three roles sent in every launch; the sample lesson is the proof and the deadline is a courtesy reminder.
structure.big_idea: Let the product sell itself with a free taste; the last-chance email is short and polite.
structure.close: Last Chance email: a short reminder of the closing time with one link.
structure.voice_notes: Conversational storytelling (pop-culture anecdotes) bridging to a plain offer.

results.detail: Vendor-stated figures on the sales page: Big Reveal '$82,358' (Success Triggers launch); Free Taste '$28,721' (How to Talk to Anybody); Last Chance '$165,803 in a few hours' (Zero to Launch funnel); the trio '$379,643' in the example launch; Mental Mastery launch '$617,944 in about a week, with over 60% of revenue from the Power Trio'; 'over $5,000,000' through an evergreen funnel. No list sizes given.

lessons: Launch email roles the standard can name: reveal, sample, last chance; the sample email is the proof block of the sequence.
The last-chance email earned the largest share of stated revenue while being the shortest; cart-close copy is 30-80 words with one link.
Related: GrowthLab's gated '5-day email funnel that generated $400,000 from a single launch' (https://growthlab.com/400k/) for the same company; emails not public.
notes: Emails shown only as images on a sales page for a paid course; annotation is from the page copy. All numbers are the vendor's.

title: Product Launch Formula open-cart email sequence (5-7 days) as described by Systeme.io
funnel_position: launch: prelaunch content, open cart, mid-cart, cart close (sequence roles: launch prelaunch, open cart, cart close)
excerpt: Article description (no email text is public): Day 1 two emails, 'cart open' then a 'tsunami' email about strong sales that must stay 'truthful and not lie about your numbers'; Days 2-4 one to two emails a day; Day 5 three emails: closing soon, launch story, final call.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a course to a list that has consumed three prelaunch content pieces on the promise that the opportunity is open for a defined window, because a dated open and a dated close, with proof and objection emails in between, concentrate buying on day one and the last day.
structure.hook: Day-1 'cart is open' announcement, then a same-day momentum email.
structure.mechanism: Three prelaunch pieces (opportunity, transformation, ownership) preceded by a 'shot across the bow' survey email; open cart 5-7 days with case study, FAQ, tour, new-bonus and scarcity emails; three emails on close day.
structure.big_idea: A launch is a sequence with a defined start and end, not a single sales email.
structure.close: Day 5: 'closing soon' in the morning, a launch story, then a final call.

results.detail: Systeme.io states 'most sales happen on day one and peak on the last day' with no figures; Walker's own emails and numbers are not public. Article's figures ('$1 Billion in sales' helped students gain) are biography, not email results.

lessons: Sequence skeleton matches the standard's Launch 10-12 (three prelaunch; open-cart; mid-cart objection, customer story, FAQ; three close-day).
'Tsunami' email: social proof of orders is allowed only when the numbers are true; a ledger row is required for any order count.
Prelaunch survey email ('what is your top question about X?') surfaces objections for the FAQ and bonus emails.
notes: Secondary source. No Jeff Walker email text was found publicly posted; the book Launch would be the primary source. Record kept for sequence architecture only.

title: Follow-up sequence for free book offer (resend with new subject lines)

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a free book (pay shipping) to a subscriber who ignored the first email on the promise that a gift is waiting, because asking for a mailing address in the subject line makes the offer concrete and lowers resistance ('since the item is free... you can be more direct').
structure.hook: Subject line asks for the recipient's mailing address.
structure.mechanism: Resend to non-openers with changed subject lines over six days.
structure.big_idea: A free physical gift justifies direct, repeated asks.
offer_devices: multiple CTA links with different labels
structure.close: Repeated address request; long P.S. covering several points.

results.detail: No result stated on the source page.

lessons: Resend-to-non-openers with a new subject is a sequence device the standard can name for open-cart follow-ups.
A free physical item lets the copy ask directly in the subject line; claim size matches offer size.

title: OMG - stop procrastinating (Fast Company article share)
market: Entrepreneurs, coaches and copywriters who buy copywriting courses
funnel_position: daily/weekly list email driving a press placement, with share-swipe copy (sequence role: daily)
excerpt: Subject: OMG - stop procrastinating | Hey [FIRST NAME GOES HERE]! In college, I had a housemate we all wanted to kill. Not literally, but not not literally, either. I had fantasies.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells a click to (and shares of) her first Fast Company article to warm subscribers on the promise of procrastination tips from a 'born procrastinator', because a revenge-fantasy story about a non-procrastinating housemate makes the reader self-identify before the link appears.
structure.hook: 'In college, I had a housemate we all wanted to kill.'
structure.mechanism: Story of the psychopathically punctual housemate, turn ('People who don't procrastinate carry a genetic mutation that also makes them psychopaths. If you're one of those people, you won't need... my FIRST PIECE IN FAST COMPANY!'), candour about her own history (crying at Nick at Nite, ghosting her list), then copy-paste share swipes for Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter and Instagram.
structure.big_idea: I'm not faking the funk: a lifelong procrastinator's tips.
offer_devices: pre-written share swipes with merge blanks
P.S. open loop ('a couple more procrastination tips... in another email, soon')
structure.close: 'Dig it? Share it and make me look super cool. I'll love you so hard.' followed by swipe copy; P.S. promises more tips in a later email.
structure.voice_notes: First person, profane, comic timing via one-line paragraphs, pop-culture references, parentheticals, first-name merge field in greeting, sign-off 'xoLaura', P.S. and P.P.S.; standard footer explains why the reader is receiving the email and invites 'Bye Felicia' unsubscribes.

results.detail: Handpicked-emails page: '#2 ... (split test with winning subj: kill my housemate)' and received the 'Email of the Week' honour from Chris Orzechowski (The Email Copywriter, 29 Jan 2020). Collection-level claim: 'All got great engagement (clicks, replies, and, where applicable, purchases).' No figures.

losing_variants.description: Subject line 'OMG - stop procrastinating' (the archived version)
losing_variants.result: Lost the split test to 'kill my housemate' per the author; margin not stated.

lessons: The story-specific subject ('kill my housemate') beat the topical imperative ('stop procrastinating'): write the subject from the body's most concrete line.
Candour as proof: admitting past failure ('I was ghosting my list on the regular') earns the right to give tips.
Share-swipe copy with fill-in blanks is a device for press-placement emails; one link repeated, no second offer.
notes: Full text read from the ConvertKit archive (ckarchive.com). Body about 870 words before the standard footer. Image in email is a screenshot of the article.

title: Uh, bye! (Not you, [FIRST NAME])
funnel_position: list email about unsubscribes, linking to a blog post on 'value' (sequence role: daily)
excerpt: Subject: Uh, bye! (Not you, [FIRST NAME GOES HERE]) | Hey [FIRST NAME GOES HERE]! The last email I wrote got more unsubscribes than usual. Not a whole lot more, just 10 people more.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells list loyalty and a click to her 'V Word' post to subscribers on the promise that entertaining stories are value, because she reports her own unsubscribe numbers candidly and argues an un-put-downable story is the highest value.
structure.hook: 'The last email I wrote got more unsubscribes than usual.'
structure.mechanism: Candid metrics (21 unsubscribes per email on average, list grown from ~4k to just under 10k), a binge-watching anecdote ('Dead To Me') as the definition of value, a coaching-client question about acceptable unsub rates, then the stance 'I'm not for everyone and don't want to be.'
structure.big_idea: Value is a story you can't put down, not a lesson.
offer_devices: P.S. open loop about husband's restaurant project
structure.close: 'I'm so happy to have you here! Please stay as long as you want.' then back to 'Killing Eve'; P.S. sets up a running theme.
structure.voice_notes: First person, profane, comic timing via one-line paragraphs, pop-culture references, parentheticals, first-name merge field in greeting, sign-off 'xoLaura', P.S. and P.P.S.; standard footer explains why the reader is receiving the email and invites 'Bye Felicia' unsubscribes.

results.detail: Talking Shrimp's handpicked-emails page states of the collection: 'All got great engagement (clicks, replies, and, where applicable, purchases).' No per-email figures.

lessons: Report your own list numbers plainly; specifics (21 unsubs, 4k to 10k) carry the argument.
An email with no offer still sells the relationship by polarizing: 'I'm not for everyone and don't want to be.'
notes: Full text read from ckarchive. Mentions her group coaching program Shrimp Club without a link.

title: Sell me, please (Hamptons house hunt)
funnel_position: list email, lesson on selling, with P.S. links to prior stories (sequence role: daily)
excerpt: Subject: Sell me, please | Hey [FIRST NAME GOES HERE], My husband, Steven, and I decided to look for a summer house out here on Long Island (where we've been renting since May)... ...and I think we already found one!

structure.argument_sentence: This sells the permission to sell to copy-shy entrepreneurs on the promise that buyers want to be convinced, because a scene with two realtors steering her back to the house she already wants shows that 'people don't like to be sold' is false when the want exists.
structure.hook: House found on the first day; 'It's on a funny-sounding street I'll call Doodlebug Lane.'
structure.mechanism: Realtor dialogue (price anchoring, '$150k' vs 'at least 300k', walk-to-village comparisons), turn: 'So, how do I feel when the broker pushes me back toward Doodlebug? I feel good! I want to be convinced... I want to be SOLD.' Then the rule: people dislike being sold what they do not want, falsely, or by someone who wouldn't recommend it; otherwise 'Sell me, please!'
structure.big_idea: People who already kinda want it want to be sold.
offer_devices: no offer; command close 'So? Go sell it.'
P.S. links to earlier story and vintage post
structure.close: 'I do, anyway. Sell me, please! So? Go sell it. xoLaura' with two P.S. links.
structure.voice_notes: First person, profane, comic timing via one-line paragraphs, pop-culture references, parentheticals, first-name merge field in greeting, sign-off 'xoLaura', P.S. and P.P.S.; standard footer explains why the reader is receiving the email and invites 'Bye Felicia' unsubscribes.

results.detail: Talking Shrimp's handpicked-emails page states of the collection: 'All got great engagement (clicks, replies, and, where applicable, purchases).' No per-email figures.

lessons: A belief-shift email: dramatize the belief ('people don't like to be sold to') in a scene, then state the corrected rule in three lines.
Price anchoring shown inside dialogue is more persuasive than stated; usable as a teaching example for the mid-cart objection email.
notes: Full text read from ckarchive.

title: "Worst I ever had" (brother-in-law sends back the fish)
funnel_position: list email with no link, lesson on critics (sequence role: daily)
excerpt: Subject: "Worst I ever had" | My husband's brother-in-law, Dan, always sends back his food. Let me first say, I hit the in-law jackpot.

structure.argument_sentence: This sells resilience to subscribers who fear criticism of their writing on the promise that complainers are a type, not a verdict, because a restaurant scene with a serial food-returner maps directly onto the reader who calls an email 'lame'.
structure.hook: 'My husband's brother-in-law, Dan, always sends back his food.'
structure.mechanism: Scripted dinner dialogue, escalating examples (risotto, short ribs, duck, fish), the chef who 'has had plenty of Dans', then the transfer: 'When someone writes back to an email and tells me it's lame... I know they're a Dan.'
structure.big_idea: There's always going to be a Dan who's just looking to send it back.
structure.close: 'When someone doesn't like something you did... remember that... All that said, remember: I love Dan. xoLaura ps FUCK THE DUCK.'
structure.voice_notes: First person, profane, comic timing via one-line paragraphs, pop-culture references, parentheticals, first-name merge field in greeting, sign-off 'xoLaura', P.S. and P.P.S.; standard footer explains why the reader is receiving the email and invites 'Bye Felicia' unsubscribes.

results.detail: Handpicked page: 'World's worst fish (split tested with winning subj: "worst I ever had")'; the archived email carries the winning subject. Collection-level engagement claim only.

losing_variants.result: Lost the split test to '"Worst I ever had"' per the author; margin not stated.

Zero-link story emails exist in a selling list and are tolerated because the sequence as a whole sells.

title: Why are we RUNNING? (Madrid layover)
